title: What It Takes to Build a Reliable AI-Powered Mailroom | Amera
summary: Learn how Amera Health Solutions uses AI to automate healthcare mailroom operations and claims intake for third-party administrators (TPAs) and health plans. We explain how we extract and validate claims data, classify correspondence, and combine AI with human oversight to improve claims processing accuracy and reduce administrative costs.
body_markdown:
**How we use AI in our mailroom**


Our mailroom receives a wide range of documents by mail, email, and fax, from standard CMS-1500 and UB-04 forms to handwritten correspondence, itemized bills, and Explanation of Benefits (EOB) documents. AI helps us process these documents in a few important ways:


1.


**Reading paper claims.** We turn scanned claim forms, supporting documents, and member-submitted bills into structured claim data. Each extracted field receives a confidence score, allowing us to identify information that needs additional review.


2.


**Sorting correspondence.** We classify incoming pages as claim forms, EOBs, repricing sheets, other correspondence, or blank pages. We also use information like envelope membership and page order to determine which supporting documents belong to which claim. We also flag legal, regulatory, and compliance mail, like attorney letters, subpoenas, and government agency notices.


3.


**Processing itemized bills and EOBs.** We extract line-item information from documents that don't follow a standardized claims format, turning them into structured data for cash-pay and other claims-processing workflows.


4.


**Checking accuracy before export.** Every claim goes through confidence checks before being exported to a customer's system. Claims that clear every check can be approved automatically. Everything else goes to a person for approval. This adds an extra layer of quality control before the data moves downstream.


These workflows let us process documents much faster than traditional manual data entry while maintaining visibility into how each claim was processed.


However, using AI in claims processing introduces its own challenges. A model can extract 98% of a claim correctly, but if the remaining 2% includes the wrong member ID, the claim may be unusable.


That's why we've developed four principles for how we build and deploy AI.


**1. One door for every model call**


Every request we send to an AI model, whether it's reading a claim form or sorting a letter, goes through a single internal gateway we built. It's a single point of entry that every part of our system must use to reach any model, instead of each part connecting to AI providers on its own.


By routing everything through one door, we can compare the actual cost and performance of completing a task, rather than relying on a model's advertised capabilities or pricing.


This allows us to monitor usage, compare models, control which providers can access data, and maintain consistent logging and security policies.


AI providers price their models differently, and the cost per token doesn't necessarily tell you how much a task will cost. A more expensive model might complete the same extraction with fewer tokens, making it cheaper overall. And a model that's excellent at reading standardized forms might perform poorly on handwritten correspondence.


It also makes our infrastructure easier to manage. When a better model becomes available, we can evaluate and introduce it without rebuilding individual workflows. When we need to review data access or investigate an issue, we have one place to look.


**2. Measure before believing**


New AI models are released constantly, often with impressive benchmark results. But a model that performs well on a public leaderboard isn't necessarily the best model for processing healthcare claims.


We evaluate new models using our own documents and workflows before introducing them into production.


For example, we might test how accurately a model extracts member IDs, procedure codes, dates of service, and billed amounts from CMS-1500 forms. We also look at how it handles poor-quality scans, unusual layouts, and missing information.


Accuracy isn't just about how many fields a model gets right. Different errors have different consequences.


Some of our most important improvements have come from fixing small problems. Some billers print the city, state, and ZIP code one line too low on a UB-04, which leaves the address blank on the electronic claim. A letter "O" in a group number can be read as a zero. A checkbox on a CMS-1500 might be marked just outside the box, even though it's clear what the provider meant. None of these looks like a big deal, but any of them can stop a claim, so we've built a specific fix for each one.


We also measure processing speed, cost, and how reliably a model identifies information it cannot confidently extract.


The goal isn't to use the newest or most sophisticated model. It's to use the model that performs best for the task, based on evidence from real claims.


**3. Shadow first**


There's an important difference between using AI to extract information and allowing AI to make decisions that affect how claims are processed.


We approach the latter much more cautiously.


Before introducing a new automated decision into production, we run it in *shadow mode* . This means the new process runs alongside our existing workflow without affecting the actual outcome.


For example, this is how we introduced auto-approval: deciding which claims can safely skip additional manual review.


Rather than immediately allowing a model to make that decision, we compare its recommendations against the results of our existing review process. We measure how many claims it would have incorrectly approved and how many it would have unnecessarily sent to a person.


These errors aren't equally costly. We'd much rather send a good claim for additional review than allow an incorrect claim to move downstream.


By running these comparisons over time, we can understand the model's failure modes and make informed decisions about when automation is appropriate.


We rolled auto-approval out in stages. It ran in shadow mode first, with its results tracked on our reporting dashboard. Next, it marked forms as auto-approved while our team still spot-checked each one. Only after that did we let simple packets, like a single claim form in its own packet, go through without manual review. We turn it on one customer at a time.


Some decisions stay with people no matter how confident the model is. Auto-approval holds any claim where we can't confirm the member, any multi-page claim whose totals don't balance, and claims for any customer that hasn't opted in. Legal, regulatory, and compliance mail is never auto-approved. If the model sees signs that a letter may be legal but isn't sure, it sends the page to a person instead of guessing.


The principle we follow as a team is: **before giving AI more responsibility, we need evidence that it can handle it reliably.**


**4. Augmentation, not replacement**


We think AI is most useful when it takes repetitive work off people's plates while preserving human judgment where it matters.


In a traditional mailroom, a person might spend much of their day opening documents, identifying forms, entering data, matching attachments, and checking fields for accuracy.


AI can handle much of that initial work. Instead of manually entering every field, a person can focus on reviewing the output, resolving exceptions, and handling cases that require judgment.


This is particularly valuable because claims don't always arrive in predictable formats.


A provider might submit a claim with an unusual attachment. A member might send an itemized bill that doesn't resemble a standard claim form. A document might contain conflicting information that requires investigation.


Real mail is messier than any test set. We've opened envelopes holding hundreds of claims for many different patients. We've seen cover letters that list three claims when only two are inside, rescanned duplicates of medical records, and state agency notices with 15-day response deadlines mixed in with routine claims.


We don't want AI to make up an answer when it encounters something it doesn't understand. We want it to identify uncertainty and make it easy for a person to resolve.


Today, claims that pass every check can be approved automatically, and everything else goes to a person. As we continue to evaluate our confidence scoring and review processes, our goal is to continue to reduce unnecessary manual work without compromising accuracy.


The objective isn't to remove people from claims processing. It's to let them spend less time on data entry and more time on work that actually requires their expertise.


**Building for reliability**


There's no shortage of AI models capable of reading a claim form. The harder problem is building a system that can process thousands of different documents consistently, identify its own mistakes, and produce data that customers can trust.


Reliability also means keeping documents together. A perfectly extracted claim that reaches a customer without its EOB or medical records isn't complete, so we check that supporting documents travel with the claim they belong to.


For TPAs and health plans, the value of AI isn't the technology itself. It's getting accurate claims data into existing systems faster, reducing manual work, and making it easier to manage exceptions when something goes wrong.


When customers learn how much of our mailroom uses AI, two questions almost always follow: Where does my data go? And are you training models on it?


We'll cover those in the next post.
